dossier: approved — 6 documents opened, 36 facts, 7 not found
factcheck_note: ok — 40 claims checked, 7 corrected, 1 left unverified
diagrams: ok — 3 SVG figures (SRAM and DRAM cells; memory array; bar chart of the real dram_refresh output): title, desc, caption present; bars below the threshold are marked by position, a label and a legend, not only by the second colour; the "6 transistors in the common design" note now matches D5
edit: ok — L2 reading level: average sentence length about 17–19 words (target about 20), long new sentences split; no phrases from guide 13.8; internal links, ids and claim tags resolve; sources entries no longer say "title only" for opened documents
accessibility: ok — every figure has role=img, title, desc and caption; all tables have header cells; headings h2 then h3 in order, no h1 in the fragment; no meaning by colour alone
findings: F1-20-layer2: "Reading destroys. The capacitor is tiny compared with the bit line; connecting them shares the charge" → opening a row moves the cells' charge onto the bit lines and into the sense amplifiers, destroying the data; the sense amplifiers write it back (D6 §2.2)
F1-20-layer2: "It is dense ... far more bits per chip, at lower cost per bit" → "It is small": two parts per cell instead of six; density and cost claims moved to the unverified box (D5; D6 §2.2)

F1-20-layer3: "Why both exist: SRAM is fast ... DRAM ... slower ... process tuned for its capacitors" → SRAM needs no refresh, DRAM must be refreshed; DRAM is the main memory (D4); 6T SRAM used on most commercial chips (D5); speed/cost claims to the box (D4 "DRAM", "SRAM"; D5)

F1-20-layer3: "Memories inside FPGAs and processors usually register the address or the output" → FPGA block RAM is fully synchronous (one vendor's library guide); processors not claimed (D7 RAMB18E1)

F1-20-layer3: disturbance "because DRAM cells are tiny and close together ... controllers and chips include measures" → repeated row activation can corrupt neighbouring rows; the paper measured it and evaluated counter-measures (D6 abstract, §6.3, §8)

F1-20-hardware: "A real SRAM cell is six transistors"; controller "today usually part of the processor chip ... large state machine"; firmware sentence → the common SRAM cell used on most commercial chips; DRAM banks with row buffers and ACTIVATE/READ/WRITE/PRECHARGE/REFRESH commands; controller in the processor in D6's system; firmware sentence removed (D5; D6 §2.1–2.4)

F1-20-code: "The name cell is reserved in Verilog" → confirmed for the -g2005 generation by a check run (Icarus Verilog rejects an instance named cell; -g1995 accepts it) (check run 2026-10-10 (ICARUS))
Not verified box: Layer 3 box: product facts (speed, cost per bit, manufacturing process), refresh/timing numbers and disturbance protections of real parts; exercise values of Listing 5.
Not found: SRAM faster than DRAM, DRAM cheaper per bit, DRAM made in a process tuned for capacitors (D1, D2 not opened) → unverified box.
Not found: Refresh intervals, retention, timings, row sizes, disturbance protections of real parts → unverified box (JEDEC standards and data sheets not opened).
Not found: Charge sharing between a tiny cell capacitor and a large bit line (D6 says reading destroys the data and is restored) → reworded to D6.
Not found: Memory controller "today usually part of the processor chip", "a large state machine" → limited to D6's system (controller in the processor) and the chapter's own FSM link.
Not found: Firmware must configure the memory controller before main memory can be used → removed (boot courses).
Not found: Verilog strength rules (IEEE text not opened) → stated as Icarus Verilog behaviour shown by R1.
Not found: Leakage depending on temperature; specifications with margin for the worst cell → removed; D6 §2.4 leakage mechanisms cited.
